content: This document is an updated Cochrane review that evaluates the efficacy and safety of vigabatrin (VGB) compared to carbamazepine (CBZ) as monotherapy for epilepsy. Vigabatrin has been established as an effective add-on therapy for refractory epilepsy, but its use is associated with a significant risk of visual field defects. The review aims to determine whether VGB is a safe and effective alternative to CBZ, a standard antiepileptic drug, when used as monotherapy in both children and adults. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Chinese Biomedical Database, up to July 2015. They also contacted the manufacturer of VGB and study authors for additional data. No language restrictions were applied. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that directly compared VGB and CBZ as monotherapy for epilepsy. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the included studies and extracted data. The primary outcome was the time to treatment withdrawal, while secondary outcomes included the time to achieve six-month and 12-month remission, time to first seizure, and adverse events. Results were presented as hazard ratios (HRs) for time-to-event data and risk ratios (RRs) for adverse events, both with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Five studies involving 734 participants met the inclusion criteria. However, only one study was deemed to be of good quality, while the remaining four were of poor quality. A meta-analysis could not be performed as planned due to inconsistencies in the reported outcomes across studies. The findings showed no significant differences between VGB and CBZ in terms of time to treatment withdrawal or time to achieve six-month remission after dose stabilization. However, VGB was associated with a disadvantage in the time to first seizure after randomization. Regarding adverse events, VGB was linked to a higher incidence of weight gain but a lower incidence of skin rash and drowsiness compared to CBZ. No differences were observed between the two drugs in terms of visual field defects or visual disturbances. The authors concluded that the current evidence is insufficient to determine the risk-benefit balance of VGB versus CBZ as monotherapy for epilepsy. Given the high prevalence of visual field defects associated with VGB, as reported in a previous systematic review of observational studies, VGB should be prescribed with caution and not considered a first-line treatment option. If VGB is used, frequent monitoring of the visual field is recommended. Future research should focus on understanding the mechanisms behind VGB-induced visual field defects and developing preventive strategies. Additionally, future monotherapy studies should adhere to the reporting standards set by the International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Commission and aim to improve methodological quality.
